item.title: Microsoft Announces Voluntary Exit Offer for Up to 60,000 Employees, Including AI Teams
item.description:
Microsoft Announces Voluntary Exit Offer for Up to 60,000 Employees, Including AI Teams

Microsoft is extending a voluntary buyout program to as many as 60,000 staff members across the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and India. The offer reaches a broader slice of the company’s roughly 223,000 employees and includes many teams that work on artificial‑intelligence products.

🔍 Overview

  • Voluntary exit offers are being made to up to 60,000 employees.
  • The program is intended to allow staff to leave with “financial support and career planning resources” while the company trims headcount without another round of layoffs.
  • The offer is described as “new for us” by Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Eligibility covers a wide range of groups, including:
    • AI experiences, Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance, and human‑resources teams.
    • Cloud + AI, MicrosoftAI, and corporate, external, and legal‑affairs teams (partial participation).
  • Teams not participating:
    • Marketing, commercial business, discovery and quantum, and security teams.
  • The offer is not based on age, length of service, or performance, according to an internal HR note.
  • It differs from an earlier voluntary‑retirement program that was limited to about 9,000 U.S. employees meeting a combined age‑and‑service threshold of 70.
Team Group Participation Status
AI experiences, Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance, HR Eligible (full)
Cloud + AI, MicrosoftAI, corporate, external, legal affairs Eligible (partial)
Marketing, commercial business, discovery & quantum, security Not eligible

💡 Why It Matters

  • The voluntary exit offer follows a layoff of 4,800 employees earlier in the year, primarily affecting Xbox and commercial‑sales staff.
  • Microsoft’s leadership frames the program as a way to “help people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft.”
  • The company states it may consider future voluntary exit offers “where there is a business and workforce need.”

📢 Official Statements

  • Amy Coleman wrote, “The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft.”
  • An internal HR note confirms the offer “isn’t based on age, length of service, or performance.”

📅 Recent Context

  • The voluntary exit program arrives months after the 4,800‑person layoff.
  • Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is reported to be planning new rounds of layoffs.
  • The new offer does not target Microsoft’s commercial‑sales teams, distinguishing it from the earlier retirement program.

#Microsoft #Workforce #AI

Source: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees

item.title: AI firms ramp up lobbying spend in Q3 2024 ahead of midterm elections
item.description:
AI firms ramp up lobbying spend in Q3 2024 ahead of midterm elections

It was a busy summer for AI lobbyists. Anthropic, OpenAI and Nvidia each recorded their highest‑spending lobbying quarter between July and September, collectively spending nearly $6 million on issues such as cybersecurity and child safety.

📊 Spending Overview

  • Total lobbying spend by the three AI firms in Q3 2024: ~$6 million.
  • Nvidia led the group with $2.2 million.
  • Anthropic followed with $2.1 million.
  • OpenAI spent $1.5 million.
Company Q3 2024 Lobbying Spend Notable Topics
Nvidia $2.2 million 6G networks, responsible AI design, competition policy, quantum computing, export control policy
Anthropic $2.1 million Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), AI Overwatch Act export provisions, Trump’s “Super Intelligence” executive order, Ratepayer Protection Act
OpenAI $1.5 million Copyright, cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models, AI safety oversight frameworks, antitrust protections for information sharing

🏛️ Policy Areas Targeted

  • Cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models
  • Child‑online safety (KOSA)
  • Export‑control provisions (AI Overwatch Act)
  • AI safety oversight and responsible AI design
  • Competition and antitrust issues
  • 6G network development and quantum computing
  • Energy cost allocation for data centers (Ratepayer Protection Act)

🤝 Political Context

  • Tech CEOs attended a White House lunch with President Donald Trump in late September, resulting in a “morally binding” AI safety accord.
  • Lobbying disclosures show additional behind‑the‑scenes discussions just before Trump named an AI czar and task force.
  • Democrats are expected to win back at least some control in Congress after the 2024 midterm elections, making engagement with lawmakers a strategic priority for AI companies.

📈 Comparison with Established Big Tech

  • Microsoft has spent at least $2 million per quarter since 2021.
  • Google regularly spends over $3 million per quarter, including this quarter.
  • The AI firms’ quarterly sums are therefore “not out of the ordinary” compared with long‑established Big Tech lobbying levels.

🔎 Company‑Specific Highlights

  • Anthropic released a detailed list of the bills, executive orders and topics it lobbied on in Q3, including KOSA, the AI Overwatch Act, the “Super Intelligence” executive order, and the Ratepayer Protection Act.
  • OpenAI’s lobbying appears to respond to fallout from the Hugging Face attack, covering copyright, cybersecurity, AI safety oversight, and antitrust protections for information sharing.
  • Nvidia lobbied on a range of issues across Congress and multiple federal agencies, including 6G networks, responsible AI design, competition policy, quantum computing, and export control policy.

🔮 Outlook

  • With data‑center development and AI safety on many voters’ minds, AI lobbyists’ work is likely to increase regardless of which party controls Congress next year.

#AIlobbying #OpenAI #Anthropic #Nvidia #TechPolicy

Source: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters

item.title: OpenAI safety chief resigns, warns of broken industry culture and need for nuclear‑level safeguards
item.description:
OpenAI safety chief resigns, warns of broken industry culture and need for nuclear‑level safeguards

David Robinson, the author of safety reports that accompanied every major model release at OpenAI, resigned this week and published an editorial in The Atlantic outlining his concerns about the company’s safety culture.

🔍 Overview

  • Robinson wrote the safety reports for each major OpenAI model release.
  • He resigned from his safety position at OpenAI.
  • His resignation was accompanied by an editorial in The Atlantic.
  • An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm.

⚙️ Core concerns

  • Robinson says the culture in industry is fundamentally broken.
  • He describes Silicon Valley’s operating mindset as “extreme confidence” and “perpetual sprints,” building ever larger models with “unimpeded optimism” that ignores or underestimates potential problems.
  • He argues the issue runs deeper than merely adding new rules or regulations.
  • He calls for AI companies to develop humility and look outside the insular “move‑fast‑and‑break‑things” world of tech.
  • He notes it is understandable to feel cynical about sudden warnings, but that should not cause us to discount them.

🛡️ Proposed safeguards

  • Robinson says AI needs “nuclear‑level safeguards.”
  • He likens frontier labs to nuclear power plants or busy airports, requiring layers of redundancy and careful, time‑consuming planning so that inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.

📈 Industry exodus

  • Robinson is the latest in a growing parade of researchers and safety workers who have left prominent AI firms.
  • Notable recent departures include:
    • Jacob Coxon – Anthropic (publicly warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”)
    • Robert O’Callahan – Google DeepMind
    • Bilal Chughtai – Google DeepMind
    • Josh Engels – Google DeepMind
    • Joe Benton – Anthropic
Person Company
Jacob Coxon Anthropic
Robert O’Callahan Google DeepMind
Bilal Chughtai Google DeepMind
Josh Engels Google DeepMind
Joe Benton Anthropic

💡 Why it matters

  • The series of resignations underscores growing internal alarm about AI safety.
  • Parallel concerns arise in cybersecurity: Microsoft’s Digital Defence Report 2026 notes a shift from AI assistants to semi‑autonomous attacks, with AI systems capable of leading or independently carrying out complex attack chains.
  • In controlled tests, an advanced AI system passed 32 sequential stages of a complex attack, and the median time from vulnerability discovery to exploitation has fallen below 24 hours, while large companies often need 30‑60 days to remediate critical external vulnerabilities.
  • These developments emphasize that safety warnings from insiders should be taken seriously and that robust, multi‑layered safeguards are increasingly urgent.

#OpenAI #AISafety #IndustryCulture #NuclearSafeguards #Cybersecurity
